title: CRLR/272/2014 of M/s Khatu Shyam Oils Vs Naseem Ahmed AND ANOTHER

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Compounding Application No. 1594 of 2015
IN
Criminal Revision No. 272 of 2014
M/s Khatu Shyam Oils Ö Revisionist
Vs
Naseem Ahmed & another Ö Respondents
Mr. Abhishek Verma, learned counsel for the revisionist.
Mr. Manish Arora, learned counsel for respondent No. 1.
Mr. B.M. Pingal, learned Brief Holder for the State/respondent No. 2.
Honíble Sudhanshu Dhulia, J. (Oral)
1. In this revision, respondent No. 1 ñ Naseem Ahmed
filed a complaint under Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument
Act against the applicant, which was subsequently registered
as Case No. 765 of 2013 wherein the learned Special Judicial
Magistrate, Roorkee, District Haridwar convicted the revisionist
for one year S.I. and imposed a fine of `13,70,000/- along with
interest @ 7% per annum and further `10,000/- to be
deposited in the Government Exchequer. Aggrieved by the said
order, the revisionist preferred an appeal before the learned
Additional Sessions Judge II, Roorkee, District Haridwar,
which was ultimately dismissed vide judgment and order dated
29.09.2014 and affirmed the judgment of the trial court.
Hence the revisionist preferred the present revision before this
Court.
2. At the admission stage, this Court vide order dated
17.11.2014 passed following order:-
 ìMr. Vikas Bahuguna, Advocate, present for the
revisionists.
Mr. Manish Arora, Advocate, present for the
respondent no 1.
Mr. Sidharth Bisht and Mr. K.S.Rawal, Brief Holders,
present for the State.
The accused-revisionist was convicted under Section
138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and was directed to
undergo simple imprisonment for one year along with a fine
of Rs. 13,80,000/- vide order dated 29.10.2013 passed by
Special Judicial Magistrate, Roorkee. Aggrieved against the
same, a criminal appeal was preferred by the accused-revisionist, which criminal appeal was dismissed by 2
nd

2
Additional Sessions Judge, Roorkee vide order dated
29.09.2014. Still aggrieved against the same, the accused-revisionist has preferred the present Criminal Revision.
Heard.
Admit.
Summon the lower court record.
List after the lower court record is received.
Heard on bail application.
Considering the case of the revisionist, it is provided
that the revisionist shall be released on bail on his executing
a personal bond and furnishing two sureties of the like
amount to the satisfaction of learned Magistrate, during the
pendency of the present criminal revision.
Realization of fine shall remain stayed during the pendency
of criminal revision, if the revisionist is able to deposit a sum
of Rs. 8,00,000/-,before the Trial Court, within four weeks
from today.î
3. Since the revisionist did not comply the order of this
Court (referred above), therefore, this Court vide order dated
08.04.2015 passed following order:-
ìMr. Vikas Bahuguna, Advocate present for the
revisionist.
Mr. Raman Kumar Sah, Deputy Advocate General
with Mr. Kuldeep Rawal, Brief Holder present for the
State.
Mr. Manish Arora, Advocate present for the
respondent no.3.
On 17.11.2014, when the present criminal revision
was taken up for admission, this Court directed, among
other things, that the realization of fine shall remain
stayed during the pendency of criminal revision, if the
revisionist is able to deposit a sum of Rs.8 Lakhs before
the trial court within four weeks.
The revisionist is not able to do so despite lapse of
time. The said order is accordingly vacated paving way for
the court below to realize the amount of fine from the
revisionist.
List this matter after four weeks.î
4. Now, at this belated stage of revision, a joint
application for compounding has been moved by the
accused/revisionist as well as complainant/respondent No. 1.
Now, after the amendment, the offence contained under
Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument is also made
compoundable offence. However, strictly speaking from the

3
perusal of the procedure under Section 320 Cr.P.C. it is not
clear whether it is applicable in an offence under Section 138
of Negotiable Instrument Act, nor it is clear at what stage the
matter is compoundable. Such guidelines have been made by
the Honíble Apex Court in Damodar S. Prabhu Vs Sayed
Babalal H. reported in 2010 (2) SCC (Cri) 1328. The said
guidelines are as follows:-
 ìTHE GUIDELINES
(i) In the circumstances, it is proposed as follows:
(a) That directions can be given that the writ of
summons be suitably modified making it clear to the
accused that he could make an application for
compounding of the offences at the first or second
hearing of the case and that if such an application is
made, compounding may be allowed by the court
without imposing any costs on the accused.
(b) If the accused does not make an application for
compounding as aforesaid, then if an application for
compounding is made before the Magistrate at a
subsequent stage, compounding can be allowed
subject to the condition that the accused will be
required to pay 10% of the cheque amount to be
deposited as a condition for compounding with the
Legal Services Authority, or such authority as the
Court deems fit.
(c) Similarly, if the application for compounding is made
before the Sessions Court or a High Court in revision
or appeal, such compounding may be allowed on the
condition that the accused pays 15% of the cheque
amount by way of costs.
(d) Finally, if the application for compounding is made
before the Supreme Court, the figure would increase
to 20% of the cheque amount.î
5. The revisionist - Sri Adesh Kumar (sole proprietor)
and the complainant/respondent No. 1 ñ Naseem Ahmed are
present in the Court today, who have been identified by their
counsels. The revisionist as well as the complainant made a
joint statement before the Court that they have arrived at
understanding and wish to compound the offence. Learned
counsel for the complainant/respondent further submits that
considering the financial condition of the revisionist, he is
agreed to take lesser amount than the actual amount of `11.00

4
lakh (Rupees Eleven lakh only) from the revisionist on which
the matter has been compounded. Further the Honíble Apex
Court in Damodar S. Prabhu (Supra) has held as under:-
ìEven though the imposition of costs by the
competent court is a matter of discretion, the scale of
costs has been suggested in the interest of uniformity.
The competent court can of course reduce the costs with
regard to the specific facts and circumstances of a case,
while recording reasons in writing for such variance.î
6. Considering the fact that the revisionist is not in a
position to make any payment of cost, as informed by the
counsel for the revisionist, this Court imposing `200/- as fine
on the revisionist, which shall be deposited before the Registrar
General of this Court within three weeks from the receipt of
certified copy of the order. The registry shall then transfer the
said amount to the State Legal Services Authority.
7. In view of the fact that since both the parties have
entered into compromise, particularly in view of the law laid
down by the Honíble Apex Court (referred above), the
compounding application is hereby allowed. The impugned
judgment and order dated 29.09.2014 passed by the learned
Additional Sessions Judge II, Roorkee, District Haridwar in
Criminal Appeal No. 152 of 2013 and order dated 29.10.2013
passed by Special Judicial Magistrate, Roorkee, District
Haridwar are hereby set aside.
8. The criminal revision stands disposed.
(Sudhanshu Dhulia, J.)
02.11.2015
JKJ
